papers.title: miR-615-3p targets SESN2 to inhibit neuronal mitophagy in an in vitro Alzheimer’s disease model by regulating the AMPK/ULK1 axis
papers.summary: This study examines how a small RNA molecule called miR-615-3p interferes with mitophagy, the process by which neurons clear out damaged mitochondria, in a cell-based model of Alzheimer's disease. The researchers found that miR-615-3p blocks a protein called SESN2, which normally helps activate the AMPK/ULK1 signaling pathway that triggers mitophagy. By suppressing this pathway, miR-615-3p leads to an accumulation of damaged mitochondria in neurons, which may contribute to the neuronal dysfunction seen in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.why: This paper provides a specific molecular mechanism (miR-615-3p/SESN2/AMPK/ULK1 axis regulating neuronal mitophagy) directly relevant to understanding mitophagy dysregulation in neurodegenerative disease, which is central to the PhD project's focus on mitophagy in neurons.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitophagy flux markers (e.g., LC3-II, p62, mitochondrial membrane potential) and AMPK/ULK1 phosphorylation levels across control, AD model, and miR-615-3p knockdown/overexpression conditions.

papers.title: Exercise and Mitophagy in Cerebral Ischemia: Mechanistic Evidence, Exercise Strategies, and Translational Challenges.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how exercise influences mitophagy, the process cells use to clear damaged mitochondria, in the context of cerebral ischemia (stroke). It discusses the molecular mechanisms linking physical activity to improved mitochondrial quality control in the brain after ischemic injury. The review also covers different exercise protocols studied and the challenges in translating these findings from animal models to clinical practice.
papers.why: Although focused on stroke rather than neurodegeneration broadly, this review could offer useful mechanistic insights into mitophagy regulation in neurons that may inform the PhD project's core focus on mitophagy and autophagy pathways in brain tissue.
papers.figure: A schematic diagram illustrating the proposed molecular pathways linking exercise-induced signaling to mitophagy activation in neurons post-ischemia.

papers.title: The N6-methyladenosine (m6A) reader YTHDF3 increases PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy by facilitating prohibitin 2 (PHB2) translation to promote retinal ganglion cell damage in diabetic retinopathy.
papers.summary: This study shows that an RNA-modifying protein called YTHDF3 reads N6-methyladenosine marks on mRNA to boost production of a protein called PHB2. More PHB2 then enhances PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, a process that clears damaged mitochondria. In diabetic retinopathy, this excessive mitophagy appears to harm retinal ganglion cells, contributing to neuronal damage in the eye.
papers.why: This paper offers a concrete molecular example of how m6A-regulated translation controls PINK1/Parkin mitophagy in neurons, directly relevant to understanding mitophagy mechanisms that could extend to interneuron biology in the brain.
papers.figure: Figure showing YTHDF3 knockdown/overexpression effects on PHB2 levels, mitophagy markers (LC3, PINK1, Parkin), and retinal ganglion cell viability/death in diabetic retinopathy models.

papers.title: Tributyl phosphate disrupts neuronal autophagy: potential involvement of TLR4 in cell and rat models.
papers.summary: This study investigates how tributyl phosphate, a common organophosphate flame retardant, affects autophagy in neurons using both cell culture and rat models. The researchers propose that TLR4, a key immune signaling receptor, may play a role in mediating this disruption. The findings suggest environmental chemical exposure can interfere with neuronal self-cleaning processes through an inflammation-related pathway.
papers.why: This relates to the profile's focus on neuronal autophagy dysregulation, offering insight into environmental and inflammatory mechanisms that could inform broader studies of mitophagy/autophagy disruption in brain tissue.
papers.figure: Figure showing autophagy marker (e.g., LC3-II/p62) changes in neurons with and without TLR4 inhibition after tributyl phosphate exposure.

papers.title: The pathological roles of intrinsically disordered proteins in lysosomal acidification dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), such as alpha-synuclein, tau, and other aggregation-prone proteins, can interfere with lysosomal acidification in neurons. Lysosomal acidification is essential for enzyme activity and proper degradation of cellular waste, including damaged mitochondria and protein aggregates. The authors argue that disruption of this acidification process is a common pathological mechanism linking several neurodegenerative diseases.
papers.why: Since lysosomal acidification is required for completing mitophagy and autophagy, understanding how disordered proteins impair this step provides mechanistic insight directly relevant to the project's focus on neuronal mitophagy dysfunction.

papers.title: Revisiting Inherited Metabolic Diseases (IMDs) Through the Lens of Selective Autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper examines Inherited Metabolic Diseases (IMDs) from the perspective of selective autophagy pathways, which specifically target damaged organelles or protein aggregates for degradation. It likely discusses how defects in selective autophagy mechanisms, including mitophagy, contribute to the pathology of various metabolic disorders. The review probably synthesizes evidence linking disrupted cellular quality control systems to disease progression, offering a new conceptual framework for understanding these conditions.
papers.why: This review likely provides mechanistic insights into selective autophagy and mitophagy pathways that are directly relevant to understanding neuronal autophagy dysfunction in the brain.

papers.title: Autophagy in Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumors (PitNETs): Molecular Mechanisms, Secretory Homeostasis, Therapeutic Resistance, and Translational Perspectives.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how autophagy operates in pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs), a type of tumor arising from hormone-secreting cells in the pituitary gland. It discusses the molecular pathways involved, how autophagy helps maintain normal secretory function, and how it contributes to resistance against therapies. The authors also explore potential translational applications, such as targeting autophagy for better treatment outcomes.
papers.why: While focused on a peripheral endocrine tumor rather than neurons, the paper's detailed treatment of autophagy pathway mechanisms and their role in cellular secretory homeostasis may offer conceptual parallels or methodological insights relevant to studying autophagy/mitophagy regulation in neurons.

papers.title: Dose-Dependent Autophagic Dysfunction and CCR5-Mediated Neuroinflammation Drive Arsenic Trioxide-Induced Cortical Neurodegeneration in Mice.
papers.summary: This study investigates how arsenic trioxide exposure affects the mouse brain cortex, finding that it causes dose-dependent problems with autophagy, the cell's waste-clearing machinery. The toxic effects appear linked to CCR5, an immune signaling receptor, which triggers neuroinflammation and contributes to neuron damage and death. Together, these processes drive cortical neurodegeneration, suggesting arsenic trioxide harms the brain through combined disruption of cellular cleanup systems and inflammatory immune responses.
papers.why: This paper demonstrates a concrete example of autophagic dysfunction driving neurodegeneration, directly relevant to understanding mitophagy/autophagy failure mechanisms in neurons that could inform spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic studies of toxin- or disease-induced cortical damage.
